title: Sa'di's Rose Garden
hookLine: a book of short tales and sayings on kings, dervishes and manners (Gulistan)
tomorrow: what's a prayer worth if you've just broken someone's heart?

lines: AN UNJUST KING ASKS A POET.
cards: Asking for prayers is easy now: a text, a post, keep me in your prayers. Sa'di tells of a king who asked in person.

In his Gulistan, the Rose Garden, Sa'di is sitting in the great mosque of Damascus, by the shrine of the prophet Yahya, the one Christians call John the Baptist. A king walks in, an Arab ruler known for being unjust.

He prays, then turns to Sa'di: pray for me, he says, I'm afraid of a powerful enemy. Sa'di's answer isn't a prayer. It's advice: show mercy to the weak under you, and you won't suffer from a strong enemy.

teach.b: Then Sa'di adds lines of verse, and they've traveled far beyond that mosque. In plain English: the children of Adam are limbs of one another, made from one essence.
When the days bring pain to one limb, the other limbs can't stay at rest. If the pain of others leaves you untouched, you don't deserve to be called human.

teach.h: THE HADITH: BELIEVERS AS ONE BODY.
teach.b: Behind those lines sits a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim: the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, compared the believers to one body; when one part aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever.

teach.h: WIDENED TO EVERY CHILD OF ADAM.
teach.b: Sa'di takes that picture and widens the circle to every child of Adam. One human family, one body. That's the Gulistan's way.

teach.h: SHORT TALES, A FEW LINES OF VERSE.
teach.b: It's a garden of tales: short stories in prose, each with a few lines of poetry tucked in, on the ways of kings, the manners of dervishes, contentment, silence, love, and how to talk to people.
The stories are small and quick, and they land like a friend's advice.
The king came for a prayer that would protect him. Sa'di sent him back to the people under his care.

how: Persian-speaking families and schools teach the Gulistan's tales and verses, and the lines on the children of Adam are recited as a call to care for every human being.

s: the lines about the children of Adam are a modern slogan
they're Sa'di's, in the Gulistan, said to an unjust king in Damascus.
Sa'di spoke them to comfort a kind and fair king
the king was known for being unjust, and afraid of an enemy.
Sa'di widens a hadith about believers as one body to every child of Adam

games.q: a new coworker's family lives where an earthquake just hit. you barely know her. what fits the Rose Garden?
o: wait; you're not close enough for it to be your place.
send a short, real message, and ask if she needs anything.
post about the earthquake online so people know you care.
games.why: when one limb hurts, the others can't stay at rest. Sa'di sends the king to the people right in front of him.

practice: Rest two fingers on your wrist, or a hand on your chest, until you find your pulse. One heart is keeping every part of you going.
As you feel it, bring to mind someone hurting far from you, someone you'll likely never meet, and keep them in view for a few beats.

wordCard.voice: Sa'di's Rose Garden: the Gulistan, a book of short tales with verse tucked in, home of the lines about the children of Adam as one body.

orig.note: Persian: Gulistan, the rose garden; the name of Sa'di's book of tales.

carryVoice: Keep this close: a garden of tales, where every child of Adam is a limb of one body. Poets, three of six.
